stem: Larkspur Lane Bakery in Castlemaine takes wholesale orders by phone and writes them on paper. Orders are often misread, and each week some cafés receive the wrong quantities. The owner decides to have an ordering program developed. Which option best describes the reason for this project?
options: An opportunity: new technology lets the bakery move into a new market
A need: a new law requires the bakery to report its wholesale sales
A problem: the current paper process causes errors in the orders
A constraint: the bakery's budget limits what the program can do
explanation: The current process is falling short: misread orders lead to wrong quantities. A project that fixes a process that isn't working responds to a problem.
whyWrong: Nothing in the scenario involves a new market; the bakery wants to fix errors in its existing orders.
No legal duty is mentioned; the driver is errors in the current process.
A constraint limits a solution; it isn't the reason the project is undertaken.

stem: Wombat Hollow Early Learning in Ararat keeps paper sign-in sheets that staff find quick and accurate. Under a new government rule, the centre must now submit its attendance records electronically every week. The director decides to have attendance software developed. Which option best describes the reason for this project?
options: It responds to a need: the centre must meet a new reporting duty
It responds to a problem: the paper sheets record attendance inaccurately
It takes an opportunity: electronic records would attract more families
It sets the scope: the centre is choosing which records to include
explanation: The paper sheets work well, so nothing is failing. The centre must now do something it can't do with its current system, which is a need.
whyWrong: The scenario says the sheets are quick and accurate, so the current process isn't failing.
Attracting families is not the driver; the centre must act because of the new rule.
Scope sets what a solution will and won't do; it isn't the reason the project happens.

stem: Quenby's Café in Warragul serves customers quickly at the counter and has no complaints about its service. The owner notices that most customers carry smartphones and that no nearby café lets customers order ahead, so she commissions an order-ahead app. Which option best describes the reason for this project?
options: A problem, because the counter ordering process isn't working as it should
An opportunity, because new technology lets the café gain an edge on rivals
A need, because the café is legally required to accept orders through an app
A functional requirement, because customers must be able to order ahead
explanation: The current process works and no obligation forces a change. The owner is choosing to use technology her customers already carry to gain an advantage, which is an opportunity.
whyWrong: The scenario says service is quick and there are no complaints, so nothing is failing.
No legal duty appears in the scenario; the café is choosing to act.
A functional requirement states what the app must do, not why the project is undertaken.

stem: A manager at Firetail Heating and Cooling in Traralgon wrote four statements about a planned dispatch program. Which statement describes the reason for the project, rather than a requirement or a constraint?
options: The program must let staff search service jobs by customer name.
The program must run on the existing Windows computers in the office.
The program must return the results of a search within two seconds.
Staff enter each service job three times, causing errors and delays.
explanation: Entering every service job three times, with the errors and delays that causes, describes a problem with the current process. That is why the project is undertaken; the other statements describe what the solution must do or the limits it must work within.
whyWrong: This is a functional requirement: it states something the program must do.
This is a technical constraint: it limits the hardware the program must run on.
This is a non-functional requirement: it sets how quickly the program must respond.

stem: Staff at Wagtail Party Hire in Bairnsdale record returned equipment on paper, and about one customer in ten is charged for the wrong number of hire days. The owner commissions a program to record hires and returns. Which evaluation criterion would best show whether the project has achieved its purpose?
options: Under 1 in 100 customers are charged for the wrong number of days
The program runs on the shop's laptop and also on the owner's own phone
Staff rate the program's colours and screen layout at least 4 out of 5
The program is finished on time and within the owner's budget of $7000
explanation: The project exists to fix a problem: customers are charged for the wrong number of hire days. A criterion that measures how often this still happens once the program is in use shows directly whether that problem has been fixed.
whyWrong: Running on several devices is a portability quality. It says nothing about whether customers are now charged correctly.
Staff opinions of the colours and layout don't measure whether the billing errors that prompted the project have stopped.
Meeting the deadline and budget judges how the project was run, not whether the program fixed the billing errors.

stem: Two florists, one in Kyneton and one in Sale, commission the same online ordering app. At the Kyneton florist, paper order slips are often lost, so some bouquets are never made. At the Sale florist, orders are recorded reliably, but the owner wants to reach customers who would rather order online. Each project is classified as responding to a problem, a need or an opportunity. Which statement is correct?
options: Both projects fix a problem, because both apps replace the old process
Both projects take an opportunity, because both use new technology
Kyneton's project fixes a problem and Sale's takes an opportunity
Kyneton's project meets a need and Sale's takes an opportunity
explanation: The reason for a project depends on the organisation's situation, not on the software it commissions. Kyneton's current process is failing (lost order slips mean some bouquets are never made), so its project responds to a problem. Sale's process works well, and the owner is choosing to reach new customers, so its project takes an opportunity.
whyWrong: Sale's orders are recorded reliably, so nothing is failing there; replacing a process that works isn't fixing a problem.
Kyneton's order slips are being lost, so its project is about fixing a failing process, not gaining an advantage.
Nothing new requires Kyneton to change; its current process is failing (order slips are lost), which makes the reason a problem, not a need.

stem:
Kurrajong Regional Library has four branches around Horsham. Its four-year plan commits the library to letting members reserve and renew items online by the end of 2027. At present, members reserve and renew items by phoning a branch. Staff handle these calls quickly, and the library doesn't expect an online service to save staff time or money. The library engages a developer to build an online system for reserving and renewing items.

The study design lists four reasons why individuals and organisations undertake software development projects. Which of them does this project mainly show?
options: Increasing productivity and efficiency
Reducing costs
Identifying opportunities to address gaps in the market
Meeting organisational objectives or needs
explanation: The library's own plan sets a target it hasn't yet met: online reservations and renewals by the end of 2027. The phone process works, and no savings of time or money are expected, so the project is undertaken to meet an organisational objective.
whyWrong: Staff already handle the calls quickly, and the library doesn't expect the system to save staff time.
The library doesn't expect the system to save money, so lower costs aren't driving the project.
The library isn't creating a product for users that no existing product serves; it is meeting a target in its own plan.

stem: Which of the following would a project brief normally include?
options: Pseudocode for each of the modules in the solution
The client's background and the problem to solve
A test table of inputs and their expected outputs
A data dictionary giving each field's data type
explanation: A brief sets out the context: who the client is and the problem, need or opportunity to be addressed. Detailed design and testing documents come later.
whyWrong: Pseudocode is a design tool, produced after analysis.
Test tables belong to development and testing, not to a brief.
A data dictionary is a design tool, produced once the requirements are known.

stem: Mei is writing a brief for Silvergull Kayak Hire in Lakes Entrance. Which sentence belongs in the brief?
options: The booking form will use a date picker and a drop-down list of kayak types.
Test 4: a hire date of 31/02/2027 should be rejected as an invalid date.
Phone bookings are often lost, so kayaks sit unused on the busiest days.
Store kayakType as a String of up to 20 characters in the bookings file.
explanation: A brief describes the current situation and the problem the business faces. Lost phone bookings that leave kayaks idle are exactly that.
whyWrong: This is a design decision, shown in a mock-up after analysis.
This is test data for a test table, prepared during development.
This is a data dictionary entry, which is a design tool.

stem: What is the main purpose of a project brief?
options: To record the tasks, durations and dependencies needed to finish the project
To judge how well the finished solution has met the client's goals
To specify precisely every requirement that developers design and test against
To set out the context and the problem, need or opportunity before analysis
explanation: A brief is the starting point for a project. It describes the context, the problem, need or opportunity, and what the solution should achieve, so the developer knows what to analyse.
whyWrong: This describes a Gantt chart, a project management tool.
This describes evaluation, which happens after the solution is developed.
This describes an SRS, which is produced after analysis.

stem:
Tahlia, a developer, has drafted this brief for Kanyana Valley Junior Football League:

*The league's 40 volunteer coaches record training attendance on paper and email it to the registrar each week. Records often arrive late or incomplete, and the registrar spends hours chasing them. The proposed users are the coaches, who will record attendance on their phones at training, and the registrar, who will check it on the office computer. None of the free team apps the league has tried sends attendance straight to the registrar. Tahlia estimates the app will take eight weeks and cost $4200, so it can be ready before the season starts in April, within the league's $5000 budget.*

Which statement about this brief is correct?
options: It is incomplete, because it doesn't state the programming language to be used.
It is incomplete, because a brief must include a data dictionary for attendance.
It is incomplete, because it doesn't explain what makes the app original.
It is really an SRS, because it states a cost and a delivery date for the app.
explanation: The study design lists these features of a brief: an outline of the problem, need or opportunity, the proposed users, the programming languages to be used, feasibility and originality. Tahlia's brief outlines the problem (late and incomplete records), names the proposed users (the coaches and the registrar), shows feasibility (her estimate fits the budget and the time before April) and originality (no app the league has tried does this). It never says which programming language will be used.
whyWrong: A data dictionary is a design tool, produced after analysis; a brief doesn't need one.
The brief says no free team app the league has tried sends attendance straight to the registrar; that is how it covers originality.
The estimate and the April date show the project is feasible, which is a feature of a brief; an SRS is the detailed specification produced by analysis.

stem: The brief for Blue Tongue Bushwalking Club's walk booking app in Daylesford says that most members are retirees over 65, and that many have poor eyesight or little experience with apps. How will this detail most help the developer during analysis?
options: It sets the scope, because features older members won't use are left out
It gives the evaluation criteria, so no data needs to be collected from members
It tells the developer which programming language will suit older users best
It shows who to collect data from and points to key usability requirements
explanation: A brief identifies the proposed users and their characteristics. Knowing that most members are older, with poor eyesight or little experience with apps, tells the developer which group to collect data from, and how, and points to usability requirements, such as large text and few steps, that analysis will make measurable.
whyWrong: Scope is agreed during analysis from what the club needs; the members' ages alone don't settle which features are included.
User details don't replace data collection. The developer still has to find out what members need, and criteria come from those requirements.
The members' age and eyesight shape usability requirements, such as large text; they don't decide which programming language the brief names.

stem:
The committee of Greenhood Tennis Club in Moe gives a developer this brief:

*Build an app with a login screen, a calendar, a leaderboard and a chat page. Use the club's green and gold colours throughout.*

What is the most important weakness of this brief?
options: It gives no measurable non-functional requirements for the app's features
It doesn't describe the club or the problem the app is meant to address
It doesn't include a data dictionary for the calendar and the leaderboard
It doesn't include a Gantt chart showing when each feature will be built
explanation: A brief sets out the context and the problem, need or opportunity, so the developer knows what to analyse. This one jumps straight to features and colours for the solution, but never says why the club wants an app. Without that, nothing guides data collection, and there is no way to judge later whether the app solved anything.
whyWrong: Measurable non-functional requirements are worked out during analysis and recorded in the SRS; a brief isn't expected to contain them.
A data dictionary is produced once analysis has worked out what data is needed; a brief isn't expected to contain one.
A Gantt chart is the project plan, a separate document; leaving it out isn't a weakness of the brief.

stem: Corellaway Coaches in Horsham is having a timetable app developed. The Gantt chart shows the project plan, in days. What is the shortest time in which the project can be completed?
options: 18 days
20 days
22 days
25 days
explanation: The longest chain of dependent tasks is Survey passengers (5) → Write SRS (2) → SRS approved (0) → Design mock-ups (4) → Code app (6) → Test app (3), a total of 20 days. That chain is the critical path, so the project can't finish sooner.
whyWrong: 18 days follows a shorter chain, through Interview drivers or Design data dictionary, not the longest one.
22 days adds both design tasks one after the other, but they run concurrently.
25 days adds every task's duration, ignoring tasks that run concurrently.

figures.title: Corellaway Coaches timetable app
figures.caption: Write SRS starts when both data collection tasks have finished. Code app starts when both design tasks have finished.

stem: The Gantt chart shows the plan for Corellaway Coaches' timetable app, in days. Which task could finish one day late without delaying the completion of the project?
options: Survey passengers
Design mock-ups
Interview drivers
Write SRS
explanation: Interview drivers (3 days) runs alongside Survey passengers (5 days), and Write SRS can't start until both have finished. A one-day delay to the interviews still ends before the survey does, so Write SRS starts on time and the finish date doesn't move.
whyWrong: Survey passengers is on the critical path; a one-day delay pushes back Write SRS and every later task.
Design mock-ups is on the critical path; Code app would start a day later.
Write SRS is on the critical path; every later task would start a day later.

figures.title: Corellaway Coaches timetable app
figures.caption: Write SRS starts when both data collection tasks have finished. Code app starts when both design tasks have finished.

stem: On a Gantt chart, what does a milestone represent?
options: The task on the critical path that has the longest duration of all
A task that can run at the same time as any other task in the plan
A task that must be finished before any other task is able to start
A key point in the project, such as a sign-off, that takes no time
explanation: A milestone marks a key point in a project, such as the client approving the SRS. It has zero duration, so it doesn't add to the project's length.
whyWrong: A milestone has no duration, so it can't be the longest task; it can sit on the critical path, but it adds no time to it.
Tasks that can overlap are concurrent tasks; a milestone isn't a task at all.
That describes a task every other task depends on, not a milestone.

stem: Firetail Heating and Cooling's plan for a technician app is shown in the Gantt chart, in days. Interviewing managers ends up taking 5 days instead of 2. What is the effect on the project?
options: It finishes 1 day later, and Interview managers joins the critical path.
It finishes 3 days later, because every task delay moves the finish date.
The finish date is unchanged, because Interview managers isn't critical.
It finishes 1 day later, and Observe technicians stays on the critical path.
explanation: The original critical path runs Observe technicians (4) → Write SRS (3) → SRS signed off → Design screens (5) → Develop app (8) → Alpha test (3), a total of 23 days. With 5-day interviews, the chain through Interview managers totals 5 + 3 + 5 + 8 + 3 = 24 days. It becomes the longest chain, so the project finishes 1 day later and the critical path now runs through Interview managers instead of Observe technicians.
whyWrong: Interview managers wasn't on the critical path, so only the part of the delay that makes its chain longer than 23 days moves the finish date.
A non-critical task delays the project once its chain becomes longer than the critical path, as happens here.
With 5-day interviews, the chain through Observe technicians still totals 23 days, a day less than the chain through Interview managers, so it drops off the critical path.

figures.title: Firetail Heating and Cooling technician app
figures.caption: Write SRS starts when both data collection tasks have finished. Alpha test starts when Develop app and Prepare test data have both finished.

stem: Tessa is managing the development of a booking program for a riding school in Bacchus Marsh. Her Gantt chart is shown, in days. Which tasks are on the critical path?
options: Survey parents, Write SRS, Design screens, Code booking module, Test program
Interview instructors, Write SRS, Design database, Code booking module, Test program
Survey parents, Write SRS, Design database, Code booking module, Test program
Survey parents, Write SRS, Design database, Code reports module, Test program
explanation: Add up each chain of dependent tasks. Survey parents (5) → Write SRS (3) → SRS approved → Design database (6) → Code booking module (7) → Test program (3) totals 24 days, the longest chain, so it is the critical path. Putting Design screens in place of Design database, or Interview instructors in place of Survey parents, gives a chain of 22 days, and the chain through Code reports module totals 21 days.
whyWrong: Design screens (4 days) finishes before Design database (6 days), so this chain totals 22 days while Code booking module waits for the database design.
Interview instructors (3 days) finishes before Survey parents (5 days), so this chain totals 22 days while Write SRS waits for the survey.
Code reports module (4 days) finishes before Code booking module (7 days), so this chain totals 21 days while Test program waits for the booking module.

figures.title: Riding school booking program
figures.caption: Write SRS starts when both data collection tasks have finished. Code booking module starts when both design tasks have finished. Test program starts when both coding tasks have finished.

stem: Tessa's Gantt chart for the riding school's booking program is shown, in days. She then learns that the database must be designed from the finished screen designs, so *Design database* can't start until *Design screens* has finished. Nothing else changes. What is the new minimum time to complete the project?
options: 24 days
28 days
30 days
35 days
explanation: Design database now starts when Design screens finishes at the end of day 12, instead of when the SRS is approved at the end of day 8, so it finishes at the end of day 18. Code booking module then runs from day 19 to day 25, and Test program from day 26 to day 28. The critical path becomes Survey parents → Write SRS → Design screens → Design database → Code booking module → Test program: 5 + 3 + 4 + 6 + 7 + 3 = 28 days. Design database was already on the critical path, so all 4 days of Design screens are added to it.
whyWrong: 24 days is the original plan. Design database now has to wait for Design screens, so it finishes 4 days later, and so does every task after it on the critical path.
30 days adds Design database's 6 days a second time. It was already on the critical path; the new dependency adds only the 4 days of Design screens in front of it.
35 days adds every task's duration, but Interview instructors still runs alongside Survey parents, and Code reports module alongside Code booking module.

figures.title: Riding school booking program
figures.caption: Write SRS starts when both data collection tasks have finished. Code booking module starts when both design tasks have finished. Test program starts when both coding tasks have finished.

stem: Which of the following is a disadvantage of interviews compared with surveys?
options: They don't let the interviewer ask any follow-up questions.
They produce only numerical data, which lacks detail.
They take more time per person, so fewer people take part.
They show what people do rather than what they think.
explanation: Each interview takes time to arrange, conduct and write up, so usually only a small number of stakeholders can be interviewed. A survey can reach many people in the same time.
whyWrong: Interviews allow follow-up questions; that is one of their main advantages.
Interviews mostly produce qualitative data in the interviewee's own words.
That describes observation, which records behaviour rather than opinions.

stem: At Tanbark Parcels' warehouse in Dandenong, packing an order takes staff much longer than managers expect. The managers want to find out exactly where time is lost during packing. Which data collection technique best suits this purpose?
options: Observation, because watching staff pack shows each step and each delay
Survey, because staff can rate the packing process on a scale from 1 to 5
Interview with managers, because they know how long packing should take
Survey, because anonymous answers show exactly how each order is packed
explanation: The managers need to see how packing is actually done. Observing staff reveals each step, workaround and delay directly, including steps staff might not think to mention.
whyWrong: A rating shows how staff feel about packing, not where the time goes.
Managers know the target time, but not where staff actually lose time.
A survey records what staff say they do; it cannot show each step as it happens.

stem: Fernhollow Vet Clinic in Warrnambool is replacing its booking system. Its stakeholders are 3 vets, 5 reception staff who take bookings, and about 2000 clients. Which plan best matches data collection techniques to these groups?
options: Survey the vets, interview every client, observe the reception staff
Interview the vets, observe the reception staff, survey the clients
Observe the vets, survey the reception staff, interview every client
Interview the reception staff, observe the clients, survey the vets
explanation: The three vets are few and hold detailed knowledge, so interviews suit them. Observing reception staff shows how bookings are really taken. A survey is the practical way to reach about 2000 clients.
whyWrong: Interviewing 2000 clients isn't practical, and surveying three vets gives up the chance to ask follow-up questions.
Observing vets shows little about bookings, and interviewing every client isn't practical.
Observing clients isn't practical, and surveying three vets misses detail an interview would give.

stem: Hannah surveyed 1500 members of Wanderlea Community Library in Shepparton. Most questions asked members to describe their experiences in their own words, and collating the responses is taking weeks. Next year she will collect data on the same topics again. Which change would make those results quickest to collate?
options: Replace the survey with an interview of every member who responded
Add follow-up questions so members can explain their earlier answers
Replace the survey with observation of members using the catalogue
Replace most open questions with closed ones, such as rating scales
explanation: Closed questions give fixed answers, such as a rating from 1 to 5, that can be counted and compared quickly. Open questions produce written answers that must be read and summarised one by one.
whyWrong: Interviewing about 1500 members would take far longer than collating the survey.
More open questions add more written answers, making collation slower still.
Observation shows how members use the catalogue, not their views on the same topics, and takes longer.

stem: In interviews, counter staff at Ironstone Gully Hardware in Maldon said they always check a customer's account number before charging goods to the account. When the developer later observed the counter, staff skipped this check on most busy mornings. What does this finding show?
options: Interviews are unreliable, so they shouldn't be used to collect data from staff
Observation shows what people really do, which may differ from what they say
The staff should have been observed first and interviewed only afterwards
A survey of the staff would have shown the same result as the observation
explanation: People often describe how a task should be done, or how they believe they do it. Observation records what actually happens, including shortcuts taken under pressure. Using both techniques gave the developer a truer picture than either would have alone.
whyWrong: Interviews still give useful detail, such as reasons and opinions; the finding shows the value of combining techniques, not of dropping one.
The order doesn't explain the difference; staff would still describe the check they believe they make.
A survey also records what people say they do, so it would most likely repeat the interview answers.

stem: The owner of a Swan Hill courier company designed its paper run sheets himself, and the company's 25 drivers are reluctant to criticise them to his face. The developer wants the drivers' honest views on what is wrong with the run sheets. Which technique best suits this purpose?
options: Interviews with each driver, held in the owner's office with him present
Observation of each driver while they fill in a run sheet during a shift
An interview with the owner about the complaints he has heard from drivers
An anonymous survey that drivers complete on their phones after a shift
explanation: Drivers who don't want to criticise the owner's design are more likely to answer honestly when their answers can't be traced back to them. With 25 drivers, an anonymous survey is practical, and open questions can capture what they think is wrong.
whyWrong: With the owner present and each driver identifiable, drivers are likely to hold back their criticism.
Observation shows how the run sheets are used, but not what the drivers think is wrong with them.
The owner can pass on only what drivers chose to tell him, which is the problem the developer is trying to get around.

stem: Kiewa Gums Cabins near Mount Beauty is replacing its booking system, which lets staff book the same cabin twice for the same night. Before writing the SRS, the developer wants to know how often this has happened over the past two years, and in which months. The office has kept the current system's monthly reports, which list every booking made, by cabin and date. Which data collection method best suits this purpose?
options: Interviews with the office staff, because they take the bookings and handle clashes
A survey of past guests, because many of them were affected by double bookings
Reports from the current system, because they hold every booking made in that time
Observation of the office for a fortnight, because it shows how clashes really occur
explanation: The developer needs a count over a long period. The monthly reports list every booking made, by cabin and date, so two bookings for the same cabin on the same night can be counted month by month, without relying on anyone's memory or waiting for a clash to happen. Reports show how often the problem occurred, not why; interviews or observation could then find the cause.
whyWrong: Staff can explain how clashes happen, but their memories can't give a reliable count, month by month, over two years.
Guests know only about their own stays, so they can't say how often clashes happened across all the cabins.
A fortnight may include no clashes at all, and watching now can't show how often they happened in the past.

stem: Strongbark Gym in Bendigo is having a membership program developed. Which of the following is a functional requirement?
options: The program must be finished before the gym reopens in February.
The program must calculate each member's monthly fee from their plan.
The program must display the results of a search within two seconds.
New staff must be able to use the program after one training shift.
explanation: Calculating each member's fee is something the program must do with its input data, so it is a functional requirement.
whyWrong: A deadline limits the time for the project; it is an economic constraint, not a requirement of the program.
A response time describes how well the program performs, so it is non-functional.
Ease of learning is a usability quality, so it is a non-functional requirement.

stem: Lindenvale Physiotherapy in Ballarat has listed four requirements for a new booking system. Which one is a reliability requirement?
options: Clients can book on phones, tablets and laptops through a web browser.
A new receptionist can make a booking within three minutes without help.
The system texts each client a reminder the day before their appointment.
The system runs all through clinic hours without crashing or losing data.
explanation: Reliability means the system performs consistently whenever it is needed. Staying available through clinic hours without crashing or losing data is a reliability target.
whyWrong: Working across devices through a browser is portability.
How quickly new staff can learn and use the system is usability.
Sending reminders is something the system does, so it is a functional requirement.

stem: Fernhollow Vet Clinic in Warrnambool wants a check-in kiosk for its waiting room. Which is the best-written usability requirement for the kiosk?
options: A client can check in at the kiosk within 60 seconds without staff help.
The kiosk must be friendly, attractive and easy for all clients to use.
The kiosk must record each client's arrival and print a queue number.
The kiosk should be simple to use, because many clients are in a hurry.
explanation: A usability requirement should set a measurable target for the intended users. Checking in within 60 seconds without help can be tested directly.
whyWrong: 'Friendly' and 'easy to use' can't be measured or tested as written.
Recording arrivals and printing a number is what the kiosk does, a functional requirement.
It gives a reason but no measurable target, so it cannot be tested.

stem:
A requirement for a checkout program at Pellow's Grocer in Echuca states:

*The program must display the customer's total, including GST, within one second of the last item being scanned.*

Which statement about this requirement is correct?
options: It is functional only, because it states what the program must display.
It is a usability requirement, because it lets customers see their total.
Its one-second limit is a non-functional target for response time.
Its one-second limit is a functional requirement, because it can be tested.
explanation: Displaying the total, including GST, is something the program does. The one-second limit sets how quickly it must do it. That is a performance target, a quality of the program rather than a function, so it is non-functional. A number alone doesn't decide this: 'the program can reprint a receipt for any sale in the last 90 days' is functional, because its number sets what the program does.
whyWrong: The one-second limit sets how well the program performs, which is non-functional, so the statement isn't functional only.
Showing a total is something the program does; the one-second limit concerns speed, not how easily users learn and use the program.
Being testable doesn't make a requirement functional; a well-written non-functional requirement, like this time limit, is testable too.

stem: While observing volunteers at an animal shelter in Morwell, a developer saw that new volunteers often gave up on the intake form in the current program because they couldn't find the right fields. Which requirement for the new program responds most directly to this finding?
options: A new volunteer can record an animal's intake within two minutes, without help
The program records each animal's species, age, intake date and microchip number
The program runs in a web browser on the shelter's computers and on its tablets
The program stays available for the whole of the shelter's opening hours
explanation: The finding is about how hard the form is for new volunteers to use, so it points to a usability requirement. A measurable target for new volunteers means the new program can be checked against it.
whyWrong: This is a functional requirement about what the form records. The current form already had the fields; volunteers couldn't find them.
Running on several devices is portability; the finding is about how hard the form is to use, not where it runs.
Staying available is reliability; the volunteers gave up because the form was confusing, not because the program failed.

stem:
The SRS for a Geelong dance school's enrolment app includes this requirement:

*A parent who has never used the app can enrol a child in a class within three minutes, without help.*

Which activity would best check whether the finished app meets this requirement?
options: Enter valid and invalid data in each field and compare the actual outputs
Ask the developers to time themselves enrolling children in several classes
Check that the enrolment code has no syntax errors and compiles correctly
Time several first-time parents enrolling a child, without giving any help
explanation: The requirement sets a measurable target for a particular group: parents using the app for the first time. Only timing real first-time parents as they enrol a child, without help, measures the app against that target.
whyWrong: Testing inputs checks that the app processes data correctly; it doesn't measure how quickly a new user can enrol.
The developers already know the app well, so their times say little about a parent who has never used it.
Code that compiles can still be hard to use; this says nothing about how long a new parent takes to enrol.

stem: A Warrnambool driving school has listed four requirements for its new lesson booking program. Which one is a robustness requirement?
options: The program runs through every business day without failing and gives correct totals.
A new receptionist can book a lesson within two minutes without any help.
Unexpected or invalid data entered on any screen never makes the program crash.
The program rejects a lesson shorter than 30 minutes or longer than 120 minutes.
explanation: Robustness is how well a program copes with unexpected or invalid input, and unusual conditions, without crashing. This requirement covers any unexpected data on any screen, so it sets a quality of the whole program rather than describing a particular check.
whyWrong: Working correctly, without failing, through normal days of use is reliability; robustness is about coping with the unexpected.
How quickly a new user can learn and use the program is usability.
This is a particular validation check that the program carries out, so it is a functional requirement.

stem:
The SRS for a Benalla kindergarten's enrolment program includes this requirement:

*The program rejects an enrolment form that has no emergency contact phone number.*

How is this requirement best classified?
options: Non-functional (robustness), because it stops missing data crashing the program
Functional, because checking input data is something the program must do
Non-functional (reliability), because it keeps the enrolment records correct
A constraint, because it limits the data that parents are able to enter
explanation: Functional requirements state what a program does with its inputs, outputs and processing, and the problem-solving methodology counts validating data among them. Rejecting a form with no emergency contact number is an existence check the program carries out, so the requirement is functional.
whyWrong: Robustness is a general quality of coping with unexpected input without crashing; a particular check on one field is something the program does.
Reliability is about the program working correctly and consistently over time; this statement describes a check the program performs.
A constraint limits how the solution can be developed, such as its budget or the equipment available; rejecting an incomplete form is a task the program performs.

stem:
Two statements from the requirements section of the SRS for an electrician's job-tracking app in Wangaratta are shown.

1. *Office staff can search every job the business has completed in the past eight years.*
2. *The app doesn't need to run on Windows laptops.*

Which option correctly classifies the two statements?
options: Statement 1 is functional; statement 2 is non-functional
Statement 1 is non-functional; statement 2 is functional
Statement 1 is functional; statement 2 is functional
Statement 1 is non-functional; statement 2 is non-functional
explanation: Searching completed jobs is something the app does, so statement 1 is functional; the eight-year figure only sets how far back the search reaches. Statement 2 describes nothing the app does. It concerns which platforms the app runs on, a quality of the solution, so it is non-functional.
whyWrong: A number doesn't make a requirement non-functional: searching jobs is still a task the app performs, and statement 2 describes no task at all.
Statement 2 describes no task; which platforms the app need not run on concerns where it works, which is non-functional.
Statement 1 states a task the app performs, a search; the eight-year figure only sets its range, so it remains functional.

stem: Which of the following is a constraint on a software project?
options: The solution must calculate each client's invoice total.
The solution must stay available throughout business hours.
The solution must let managers export a monthly sales report.
The solution must be developed for no more than $9000.
explanation: A budget limit restricts the project; it doesn't describe what the solution does or a quality it has. That makes it a constraint.
whyWrong: Calculating an invoice total is something the solution does, a functional requirement.
Staying available is a quality of the solution (reliability), a non-functional requirement.
Exporting a report is something the solution does, a functional requirement.

stem: The manager of Wanderlea Community Library in Shepparton says the new loans program must run on the three Android tablets already used at the front desk. How is this statement best classified?
options: A technical constraint
An economic constraint
A legal constraint
A functional requirement
explanation: The program is limited by the hardware it must run on: the existing Android tablets. A limit set by the technology available is a technical constraint.
whyWrong: Nothing in the statement limits cost or time; it limits the hardware the program must run on.
No law is involved; the limit comes from the existing tablets.
It doesn't state something the program does; it limits the platform the program must run on.

stem: Brookhollow Dental in Mildura is having a patient portal developed. The portal will store patients' names, contact details and treatment histories. Which constraint does storing this data place on the project?
options: An economic constraint: storing treatment histories will raise the cost
A technical constraint: treatment histories must be stored in a CSV file
A legal constraint: health information must be handled as privacy law requires
A functional requirement: patients must be able to view their treatment history
explanation: Patients' contact details and treatment histories are personal and health information. The clinic must collect, store and share them only as privacy law allows, which is a legal constraint on the portal.
whyWrong: Nothing in the scenario sets a budget; storing data does not in itself limit cost.
Choosing a file format is a design decision, not a limit imposed on the project.
This states something the portal does, not a limit that storing the data imposes.

stem: Tallis Creek Bowls Club in Seymour wrote four statements about its planned rink booking app. Which statement is a constraint?
options: The app will not take payments; members will keep paying at the clubhouse.
The app must be ready before the pennant season opens on 1 October.
A first-time member must be able to book a rink within one minute.
The app must show which rinks are free at a time the member chooses.
explanation: A fixed deadline limits when the solution must be delivered. It restricts the project rather than describing what the app does or a quality it has, so it is a constraint: an economic one, because economic constraints cover time as well as cost.
whyWrong: This sets the scope: what the app will and won't do.
This sets a usability target for the app, a non-functional requirement.
This is something the app does, a functional requirement.

stem: Jonah is building a website for a houseboat hire business in Echuca. He wants to use photos of the Murray River that he found through a search engine. Which approach best meets the legal constraint that applies to these photos?
options: Use the photos, as long as each one is credited to the website it came from
Use the photos, because anything published online is free for others to use
Use only photos the business owns, or has permission or a licence to use
Use the photos after cropping and recolouring them so they become new works
explanation: Photos are protected by copyright whether or not they are online. Jonah can use a photo only if the business owns it or the copyright owner has given permission, for example through a licence whose conditions he follows.
whyWrong: Crediting the source doesn't give permission; the copyright owner must still agree to the use.
Publishing a photo online doesn't remove its copyright; the photographer still owns it.
Editing someone else's photo still copies their work; the changes don't make it free to use.

stem: Amira has 8 weeks and a $4000 budget to build a booking app for a volunteer hall committee in Nhill. The whole budget pays for her own time. Her estimates show that the six features the committee asked for would take 11 weeks to build and test. Which response best works within the project's constraints?
options: Hire a second developer so that all six features are ready within 8 weeks
Agree with the committee on the most important features and defer the rest
Build all six features, and have the committee start using the app in week 11
Shorten the testing so that all six features can be built within the 8 weeks
explanation: The deadline and the budget are both fixed, so the work has to shrink to fit them. Agreeing a smaller scope with the committee delivers the most important features within 8 weeks and $4000, and the deferred features can be added in a later version.
whyWrong: The $4000 already pays for Amira's time, so a second developer would take the project over budget.
Finishing in week 11 breaks the 8-week deadline, which is a constraint on the project.
Cutting testing meets the deadline by letting more errors reach the committee; it doesn't reduce the work to fit.

stem:
A volunteer-run op shop in Stawell is having a rostering and sales program built. Two statements from the constraints section of its SRS are shown.

1. *The program must be in use before the busy pre-Christmas period starts on 1 November.*
2. *Many of the volunteers have never used a computer program at work, and some have never used a computer at all.*

Which option gives the type of each constraint?
options: Statement 1 is technical; statement 2 is social
Statement 1 is economic; statement 2 is technical
Statement 1 is technical; statement 2 is economic
Statement 1 is economic; statement 2 is social
explanation: The problem-solving methodology treats time, as well as cost, as an economic constraint, so a date by which the program must be in use is economic. Social constraints concern the users' level of expertise, so volunteers with little or no computer experience are a social constraint.
whyWrong: A deadline limits the time available, which makes it economic; technical constraints come from the technology, such as processing speed, capacity or equipment.
The users' level of expertise is a social constraint; technical constraints concern the technology, not the skills of the people using it.
A deadline is economic, not technical, and the users' expertise is social: it isn't a limit on money or time.

stem: After the scope of a project has been agreed, the client keeps asking for small extra features, and the developer adds each one without changing the schedule or the budget. Which term describes this situation?
options: A personnel change
A technical issue
Scope creep
A constraint
explanation: Scope creep is the uncontrolled growth of what a solution must do after the scope has been agreed. Each extra is small, but together they add work that the schedule and budget don't allow for.
whyWrong: A personnel change is a change in who works on the project, such as a developer leaving.
A technical issue is a problem with hardware, software or tools, not growth in the features.
A constraint, such as a budget, limits the project; the situation describes features growing beyond the agreed scope.

stem: The scope for Ironbark Gully Tool Library's app in Ararat says the app will let members browse, borrow and return tools, and will send reminders when a tool is overdue. It will not handle membership fees or tool repairs. Which requested feature falls within this scope?
options: A page where members pay their annual membership fee online
A form where volunteers log repairs made to damaged tools
A shop page that sells second-hand tools to the public
An email sent to a member when a borrowed tool is overdue
explanation: Overdue reminders are named in the scope as something the app will do, so this feature is inside the boundary.
whyWrong: Membership fees are explicitly excluded from the scope.
Tool repairs are explicitly excluded from the scope.
Selling tools isn't among the features the scope includes, so it lies outside the boundary.

stem: The scope of Gumleaf Café's ordering app in Beechworth states that the app will take takeaway orders and payments, and will not manage staff rosters. At evaluation, staff complain that the app can't produce rosters. How should this be treated?
options: Not as a failure, since rosters were excluded from the agreed scope
As a failure, as the solution doesn't meet all of the staff's current needs
As a failed non-functional requirement, as the app is less usable for staff
As an unmet constraint, as the budget limited which features were built
explanation: A solution is evaluated against what was agreed. Rosters were explicitly outside the scope, so their absence doesn't count against the app, although a rostering feature can be recommended for a later version.
whyWrong: Rostering was never an agreed requirement; the app is judged against what was agreed, not every need staff have.
Usability concerns how easily users complete the tasks the app supports, not features it was never meant to have.
Nothing suggests the budget caused this; rosters were excluded when the scope was set.

stem: Leilani is preparing the Gantt chart for a Kilmore pony club's rally booking app. Why should the scope of the app be agreed before she finalises the chart?
options: The scope sets the order of the tasks that are on the critical path
The features in scope decide which tasks are needed and their durations
The scope sets the deadline, which becomes the last milestone on the chart
Features excluded from the scope must each appear on the chart as a task
explanation: A Gantt chart plans the tasks needed to deliver the solution and how long each takes. Until the scope settles which features the app will and won't include, Leilani can't know which design, coding and testing tasks to plan, or how long the project will take.
whyWrong: The order of tasks comes from the dependencies between them, not from the scope.
A deadline is a constraint on the project, not part of the scope.
Excluded features won't be built, so no tasks are planned for them.

stem: Nell proposes a club app that will take bookings, sell merchandise, stream matches and manage player statistics. Her manager says the scope is too large for the 10 weeks available. What does the manager mean?
options: It includes more features than can be built and tested in 10 weeks
It has more non-functional requirements than can be measured in 10 weeks
It names more stakeholders than data can be collected from in 10 weeks
It needs more money than the club's budget constraint will allow for
explanation: Scope is what the solution will and won't do. Nell's covers four large features, too many to build and test in 10 weeks. Narrowing it, for example to bookings and statistics now and the rest in a later version, makes the project achievable.
whyWrong: The concern is how many features must be built, not the qualities the app must have.
Stakeholders affect data collection; scope is about what the app will and won't do.
Nothing in the scenario mentions money; the manager's concern is fitting the features into 10 weeks.

stem: The scope in the SRS for a Warburton guesthouse's app said only: *The app will manage bookings.* At handover, the owner expected the app to take deposits by card and email each guest a feedback survey after their stay, but it does neither. Which change to the scope statement would most likely have prevented this disagreement?
options: Adding a response-time target for confirming a booking in the app
Adding a deadline and a budget for developing the booking app
Listing the stakeholders who were interviewed about bookings
Stating what the app will not do, such as deposits and surveys
explanation: 'Manage bookings' can be read broadly. A scope that also says what the app will not do, such as taking card deposits or emailing feedback surveys, makes the boundary clear, so the owner and the developer agree on what will be delivered before work begins.
whyWrong: A response-time target is a non-functional requirement; it doesn't say which features are included.
A deadline and a budget are constraints; they don't say which features the app covers.
Listing stakeholders doesn't define the boundary of what the app will do.

stem: Corella Clay Studio in Castlemaine wants an app for its pottery classes. Its developer, Mei, has 9 weeks to build and test the first version of the app, and the studio's budget for it is $6500. The studio's feature list is shown. Which statement best sets the boundary for the first version?
options: Version 1 must be finished within 9 weeks and must cost the studio no more than $6500
Version 1 will include bookings, online payment and reminders; the waiting list and the gallery wait for version 2
Version 1 will include bookings, the waiting list and reminders; online payment and the gallery wait for version 2
Version 1 will be reliable and easy to use, so that students of all ages can use it on any phone
explanation: A version boundary says which features a version will include and which it leaves for later. The three essential features take 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 weeks, within Mei's 9, and neither desirable feature (4 or 3 weeks) fits in the 2 weeks left. Stating that online payment and the gallery wait for version 2 makes clear what this release won't address.
whyWrong: A deadline and a budget are constraints: they limit the project, but they don't say which features version 1 includes.
These features take 4 + 4 + 1 = 9 weeks, so they fit, but the waiting list, which the studio rates essential, is pushed back to make room for a desirable feature.
Reliability and ease of use are non-functional requirements, qualities of the app; they don't say which features are in or out.

figures.title: Corella Clay Studio's feature list
columns: Estimated time to build and test
rows: 1. Students book a place in a class
2. Students join a waiting list when a class is full
3. Students receive an SMS reminder the day before a class
4. Students pay class fees in the app
5. Visitors browse a gallery of students' work

stem: Which component can appear in a data flow diagram (Level 1) but never in a context diagram (Level 0)?
options: An external entity outside the system, such as *Customer*
A data store that holds data, such as *Bookings*
A labelled data flow, such as `booking_details`
A circle that names the whole system, such as *Booking system*
explanation: The study design gives a context diagram three components: the system, external entities and data flows. Stored data stays hidden inside the system. A Level 1 DFD opens the system up into processes and adds the data stores they use, so a data store can appear only on the DFD.
whyWrong: External entities appear on both diagrams, outside the system.
Labelled data flows appear on both diagrams.
The circle naming the whole system belongs to the context diagram; a DFD replaces it with processes.

stem: Sandpiper Cycle Hire in Geelong is having a hire system developed. The DFD for the system is shown. Which data flow breaks a DFD convention?
options: `hire_request`, from *Customer* to *Record hire*
`hire_details`, from *Record hire* to the *Hires* data store
`invoice`, from *Calculate charge* to *Customer*
`hire_report`, from the *Hires* data store to *Manager*
explanation: An external entity can't take data straight from a data store. A process must read the *Hires* data store and produce the report, for example a new process *Produce hire report* that sends `hire_report` to *Manager*.
whyWrong: An external entity may send data to a process, so this flow is correct.
A process may write data to a data store, so this flow is correct.
A process may send data to an external entity, so this flow is correct.

stem: Lantern Lane Cinema in Ballarat is having a ticketing app developed. A customer who holds a gift voucher can redeem it while booking a ticket; most customers book without one. On the use case diagram, how should *Redeem gift voucher* be linked to *Book ticket*?
options: <<extends>>, with the arrow from *Redeem gift voucher* to *Book ticket*
<<extends>>, with the arrow from *Book ticket* to *Redeem gift voucher*
<<includes>>, with the arrow from *Book ticket* to *Redeem gift voucher*
<<includes>>, with the arrow from *Redeem gift voucher* to *Book ticket*
explanation: Redeeming a voucher happens only when the customer has one, so it is optional behaviour added to booking: an <<extends>> relationship. The arrow points from the extending use case to the base use case it extends.
whyWrong: The relationship is right, but an <<extends>> arrow points to the base use case, *Book ticket*.
<<includes>> would mean every booking redeems a voucher, but most customers don't have one.
The step is optional, so <<includes>> is wrong; an <<includes>> arrow also starts at the base use case.

stem: Platypus Pool Swim School in Shepparton is having an app developed. Parents book lessons and view their child's progress, and instructors record progress after each lesson. Lesson and progress records will be stored in the app's own database. Which statement identifies a convention error in the use case diagram shown?
options: *Instructor* should be inside the system boundary, because instructors are staff
The associations need data labels, such as `progress_details`, to show what moves
*Lesson database* is drawn as an actor, but it is data stored within the system
*Record progress* should be linked to *Parent*, because parents read the results
explanation: An actor is the role of a user outside the system who interacts with it, such as *Parent* or *Instructor*. Lesson and progress records are stored within the app, so *Lesson database* is part of the system and shouldn't be drawn as an actor.
whyWrong: Actors always sit outside the system boundary, even when they are staff of the organisation.
Associations show who takes part in a use case; data labels belong on DFD data flows.
Parents don't record progress; they read it through *View progress*, which they are already linked to.

figures.title: Use case diagram: swim school app

stem: A primary school canteen in Werribee is having an online lunch ordering system developed. The DFD drawn for the system is shown. Which statement identifies a convention error in the DFD?
options: *Take order* sends data to *Parent* and to the *Orders* data store, but a process can have only one output
The *Orders* data store sends data to two processes, but a data store can be read by only one process
*Canteen staff* gets `order_list` from *Prepare order list*, but should read the *Orders* data store directly
*Calculate term charges* takes in `order_history` but sends no data to anything, so it produces nothing
explanation: Every process must turn its inputs into at least one output. *Calculate term charges* takes in `order_history` but sends nothing to an external entity, a data store or another process, so the term charges it calculates go nowhere. It needs an output flow, such as `term_statement` sent to *Parent*.
whyWrong: A process can have several outputs. Sending a confirmation to the parent and storing the order is correct.
A data store can be read by any number of processes.
This part follows the conventions: an external entity gets stored data through a process, never directly from a data store.

stem: A Ballarat gym is having a member app developed. Members book classes and pay their fees in the app, receptionists use it to book classes for members who phone the gym, and trainers record workout plans. Which statement identifies a convention error in the use case diagram shown?
options: The line joining *Member* to *Trainer* links two actors, not an actor and a use case
*Book class* is linked to two actors, but a use case can be linked to only one actor
*Receptionist* should be drawn as an external entity, because it sends booking data to the app
Use case names such as *Book class* should be nouns, like the labels on data flows
explanation: An association joins an actor to a use case the actor takes part in. Members and trainers may talk to each other, but that happens outside the app, so the line between *Member* and *Trainer* should be removed.
whyWrong: A use case is linked to every actor who takes part in it; here both members and receptionists book classes.
Sources and destinations of data are external entities on context diagrams and DFDs. On a use case diagram, a user role that interacts with the app is an actor.
A use case is named as an action, such as *Book class*, because it is a goal an actor achieves; noun labels belong on DFD data flows.

figures.title: Use case diagram: gym member app

stem: Before any screens are designed, the developer of a Lakes Entrance youth sailing club's app wants to show the committee which tasks each type of user (coach, parent and sailor) will be able to carry out. Which tool best suits this purpose?
options: A context diagram, because it shows each type of user as an external entity
A data flow diagram, because it shows each process that the app carries out
A use case diagram, because it shows each actor and the goals they achieve
A data dictionary, because it lists every field that each user will enter
explanation: A use case diagram shows the actors who interact with a system and the use cases, or goals, that each one takes part in. That is what the committee needs to see: which tasks coaches, parents and sailors will each be able to carry out.
whyWrong: A context diagram shows the data flowing between the system and each entity, not the tasks each user carries out.
A DFD shows how data moves between processes and data stores, not which user carries out each task.
A data dictionary describes the data the app stores, not what each type of user can do.

stem: A junior athletics club in Horsham is having a results system developed. Coaches enter race results, families receive results summaries and pay fees, the club's bank processes the payments, and the regional league receives the results of each meet. The system will store every athlete's details and results. Which statement identifies a convention error in the context diagram shown?
options: *Bank* should be removed, because every external entity must be a person
The flow from the system to *Regional league* has no label naming its data
The system should be split into two processes, one for results and one for fees
A data store, *Athletes*, should be added, because the system stores details
explanation: Every data flow is a labelled one-way arrow, named for the data it carries, such as `meet_results`. The flow from the system to *Regional league* has no label, so the diagram doesn't show what data the league receives.
whyWrong: External entities are users or other systems outside the system; the bank's system that processes payments is one.
A context diagram shows the whole system as one circle; processes appear only on a DFD.
A context diagram has no data stores; stored data stays hidden inside the system.

stem: Gannet Island Ferries, based in San Remo, is having a ticketing app developed. Passengers buy tickets and check the timetable on their phones. Deckhands employed by the company use a handheld scanner to scan each ticket as passengers board, and they report the number of passengers on each crossing. What does the actor marked X in the use case diagram shown represent?
options: The company, Gannet Island Ferries
The handheld ticket scanner
The ferry ticketing app
A deckhand on the ferry
explanation: An actor stands for the role of a user who interacts with the system to achieve a goal. Deckhands scan tickets and report passenger numbers, so actor X represents a deckhand and should be labelled *Deckhand*, just as the other actor is labelled with the passenger's role.
whyWrong: The company employs the deckhands, but it doesn't use the app itself; an actor names the role of the person who does.
The scanner is the device the deckhand uses to reach the app, not the role of the person interacting with it.
The ticketing app is the system itself, shown by the boundary; actors always sit outside it.

figures.title: Use case diagram: ferry ticketing app

stem: Wattle Flat Community Garden in Kyneton is having a system developed to allocate its garden plots. People apply for a plot; when no plot is free, they are put on a waiting list. The coordinator receives a summary of each plot that is allocated. Which statement identifies a convention error in the DFD shown?
options: *Coordinator* only receives data and sends none, but every external entity must both send and receive data
*Check application* reads one data store and writes to another, but a process can be linked to only one data store
The *Waiting list* data store receives data but sends none, so no process ever uses the applicants stored in it
*Check application* names its output flows differently from its inputs, but a process should pass data on under the same name
explanation: Every data store needs at least one flow coming in and at least one going out. *Waiting list* receives `waitlist_entry` from *Check application*, but no flow leaves it, so the waiting applicants are stored and never used: no one can be offered a plot from the list. A flow such as `waiting_applicants` from *Waiting list* to *Allocate plot* would fix it.
whyWrong: An external entity must send at least one flow or receive at least one; *Coordinator* receives `allocation_summary`, which is enough.
A process can read from and write to as many data stores as it needs.
The rule is the reverse: a process changes the data it receives, so the flow it sends out should have a different name from the flow that came in.

stem: At which point in a software project is the software requirements specification (SRS) produced?
options: At the end of analysis, before design begins
At the start of the project, before any data is collected
At the end of design, once the mock-ups are approved
At the end of development, before testing begins
explanation: The SRS records the requirements that analysis has identified. It must be settled before design, because designers plan the solution to meet it.
whyWrong: At the start only a brief exists; requirements aren't known until data has been collected and analysed.
Designs are based on the SRS, so it must exist before design starts.
Producing it this late would leave the design and development without agreed requirements.

stem: Rohan's team at Spinebill Linen Hire in Ballarat has finished developing an order-tracking program. A tester is writing test cases to check that the program meets the client's requirements. Which document should the test cases be based on?
options: The project brief, because it describes why the program was wanted
The Gantt chart, because it lists the tasks the team has completed
The SRS, because it sets out the requirements the program must meet
The data dictionary, because it lists every variable in the program
explanation: The SRS is the agreed record of what the program must do and the conditions it must meet, so tests of whether the program meets the client's requirements are drawn from it.
whyWrong: A brief is short and high level; it doesn't set out detailed, testable requirements.
A Gantt chart schedules project tasks; it says nothing about what the program must do.
A data dictionary describes the data items in the design, not the requirements the client agreed to.

stem: A draft SRS for Wattlebird Regional Library's loans program in Hamilton contains four statements. Which statement belongs in the SRS, rather than being a design decision?
options: Loan renewals will use a binary search of the sorted member array.
The *Renew* button will sit to the right of each loan in a table.
The renewal module will be written as a function called `renewLoan`.
Members must be able to renew a loan online before its due date.
explanation: An SRS states what the solution must do. Letting members renew loans online is a requirement; the other statements decide how it will be done, which is design work.
whyWrong: Choosing a search algorithm decides how the requirement is met, a design decision.
Placing a button is a screen layout decision made in design, for example on a mock-up.
Naming and structuring a function is a design and development decision.

stem: Blackbox Bend Caravan Park in Swan Hill is having a booking system developed. Which statement from its SRS describes the solution's technical environment?
options: Most office staff are casual workers with basic computer skills.
The system will run on the office's Windows 11 laptops and network.
The system will take site bookings but will not handle kiosk sales.
The system must be delivered within a budget of $15 000.
explanation: The technical environment is the hardware, operating system and network the solution will run on, and the office's Windows 11 laptops and network are exactly that. The other three statements belong in the SRS too: they describe user characteristics, scope and a constraint, which the study design also lists as features of an SRS.
whyWrong: This describes user characteristics (the users' level of computer skill), not where the system will run.
This sets the scope: what the system will and won't do.
A budget is an economic constraint on the project, not the environment the system runs in.

stem: Tomasz has drafted the SRS for a volunteer rostering program for Petrel Point Community Radio in Portland. The station manager, who must approve it, says she can't follow much of it because it is full of technical terms. What is the best advice for Tomasz?
options: Keep the technical terms, since the SRS is written mainly for developers
Rewrite it in plain language so the manager can check each requirement
Replace the requirements with pseudocode, which is easier to follow
Ask the manager to approve the brief instead, as it has less jargon
explanation: The client approves the SRS to confirm that its requirements are correct and complete before design begins. The manager can only do that if she understands what she is approving, so the requirements should be written in language she can follow, while staying precise.
whyWrong: Developers use the SRS, but the client must also read and approve it, so it can't be written for developers alone.
Pseudocode sets out how a module will work, which is a design decision; the SRS states what the program must do.
The brief is short and high level; the detailed requirements that must be agreed are in the SRS.

stem: The SRS for a stocktake program at Gelliondale Hardware & Timber in Yarram says the program will run on the store's existing tablets, which staff operate by touch alone, with no keyboard or mouse. Which design decision does this technical environment rule out?
options: Showing a product's details only when the pointer hovers over it
Buttons large enough for staff to tap them accurately with a finger
An on-screen keyboard for typing a code when a barcode label is torn
Saving each count as soon as staff tap the Next product button
explanation: The technical environment is the hardware and software a solution will run on, and the design must work there. With touch alone there is no mouse pointer to hover, so details that appear only on hover could never be seen. They would need to open with a tap instead.
whyWrong: Large buttons suit finger taps, so they fit the tablets the SRS describes.
An on-screen keyboard is how text is entered on a tablet that has no physical keyboard.
Tapping a button works on a touchscreen, so saving each count this way suits the tablets.

stem: Halfway through designing a class booking program for Ironbark Hollow Yoga in Heathcote, Shanti and the studio's owner agree to add a waiting list for full classes. The approved SRS doesn't mention a waiting list. Shanti has worked out the extra time and cost, and the owner has accepted them. What should Shanti do with the SRS?
options: Leave the SRS as it is, because the owner approved it before design began
Describe the waiting list only in the pseudocode for the class module
Add the waiting list to the SRS, and have the owner approve the update
Record the waiting list only in her project journal, not in the SRS
explanation: The SRS is the agreed statement of what the program must do, and designers, testers and evaluators all work from it. An agreed change must therefore be added to it, and the owner's approval of the updated SRS confirms that both sides agree. Otherwise nothing would require the waiting list to be designed, tested or evaluated.
whyWrong: An approved SRS can be updated when a change is agreed; left as it is, it no longer matches what will be built.
Pseudocode shows how a module will work; the requirement itself belongs in the SRS, where the owner can see and approve it.
A journal records progress and decisions, but testers and evaluators work from the SRS, so the requirement could be missed.

stem: Marisol is writing the SRS for a booking program for Kurrajong Paws Grooming in Kyneton. Her draft has sections for functional and non-functional requirements, constraints, scope and the technical environment. It also includes a context diagram, a data flow diagram and a use case diagram of the salon's current booking process. Which feature that the study design lists for an SRS is missing from her draft?
options: The programming languages that will be used to build it
An assessment of whether the project is feasible
Mock-ups of the main booking and payment screens
The characteristics of the staff and clients who will use it
explanation: The study design lists six features of an SRS: defining requirements, constraints, scope, user characteristics, technical environments, and analytical tools depicting existing processes and systems. Marisol's draft has all of them except the user characteristics, such as who the users are, their level of expertise and how often they will use the program.
whyWrong: The programming languages to be used are a feature the study design lists for a brief, not for an SRS.
Feasibility is a feature of a brief, which shows at the start that the project is achievable.
Mock-ups are a design tool for the design stage; they aren't one of the features the study design lists for an SRS.

stem: When is the source code of a newly written program protected by copyright in Australia?
options: Only after the code is registered with IP Australia
Only when every file displays a © symbol and the year
Only once the program has been sold or published
Automatically, once the code is written down or saved
explanation: Copyright arises automatically when original work is put into material form, which for code means written down or saved. No registration or notice is needed.
whyWrong: Australia has no copyright register; IP Australia handles patents, trade marks and designs.
A © notice can remind people who owns the code, but protection doesn't depend on it.
Unpublished code is protected too; protection starts when the code is created.

stem: Jarrah, a freelance developer, writes a stock program for Cobblestone Pottery in Daylesford. The pottery pays for the program, but the contract says nothing about who owns the code. Who owns the copyright in the code?
options: Jarrah, because the contract doesn't assign the copyright to the pottery
Cobblestone Pottery, because it paid Jarrah to write the program
Cobblestone Pottery, because the program runs on the pottery's computers
Jarrah and the pottery jointly, because both took part in the project
explanation: The author of code owns its copyright unless they wrote it as an employee as part of their job, or assigned it in writing. Jarrah is a contractor and the contract assigns nothing, so Jarrah keeps the copyright. To own the code, the pottery needed a written assignment in the contract.
whyWrong: Paying for software doesn't by itself transfer copyright; a written assignment is needed.
Where the program runs has no effect on who owns its copyright.
Jarrah alone wrote the code; setting requirements doesn't make the client a joint author.

stem: Brolga Flat Netball Association in Traralgon is having a registration app developed. Which approach best protects the privacy of players' personal information?
options: Collect every detail that might be useful later, in case new features need it
Keep players' details after they leave, so they can re-register more quickly
Collect only the details needed to register, and tell players why they're needed
Share players' details with sponsors, since players agreed to join the association
explanation: Good privacy practice is to collect only the personal information needed for the purpose and to tell people why it is collected and how it will be used. Collecting only what is needed reflects APP 3 (Collection of solicited personal information), which limits collection to what is reasonably necessary.
whyWrong: Collecting data just in case goes beyond what is reasonably necessary, the limit APP 3 sets, and adds to the harm of any breach.
Once players leave, their details aren't needed for registration; APP 11 (Security of personal information) expects information no longer needed to be destroyed or de-identified.
Joining isn't consent to passing details to sponsors; APP 6 (Use or disclosure of personal information) limits disclosing personal information for a purpose other than the one it was collected for.

stem: Mei studies a rival's booking app, then builds her own booking app for her family's dog grooming salon in Bendigo. She writes all of the code herself and designs her own screens and graphics, but her app has similar features. Which statement is most accurate?
options: She has breached copyright, because her app copies the rival's features
She hasn't breached copyright, which protects code but not ideas
She must register her app's code before she can use it in the salon
She must acknowledge the rival's developer, since her features are similar
explanation: Copyright protects the way a program is expressed, such as its code and graphics, not the ideas or features behind it. Mei wrote her own code and designed her own graphics, so she hasn't copied anything the rival's copyright protects.
whyWrong: Features and ideas aren't protected by copyright; only their expression, such as the code, is.
Copyright arises automatically; there is nothing to register before the app is used.
Mei copied no code, screens or graphics, so there is nothing of the rival's to acknowledge; similar features alone create no copyright obligation.

stem: Anika is employed full-time as a developer by Wangoom Freight Lines in Warrnambool. As part of her job, she writes a program that plans delivery routes. She later resigns and wants to sell the program to other freight companies. Her employment contract says nothing about copyright. Who owns the copyright in the program's code?
options: Anika, because she personally wrote every line of the code
Anika, because her employment contract doesn't mention copyright
The company, because Anika wrote the code as part of her job
Anika and the company jointly, as both contributed to it
explanation: When an employee writes code as part of their job, the employer owns the copyright unless an agreement says otherwise. Anika wrote the program in her job at Wangoom Freight Lines, so the company owns it, and she can't sell it without the company's permission.
whyWrong: Authors usually own the copyright in their work, but code an employee writes as part of the job belongs to the employer.
