For an employee, a contract that is silent leaves the employer as owner; it is a contractor who keeps the copyright when the contract is silent.
Employing Anika doesn't make the company a co-author; the employer owns the code outright.

stem: Ines, a freelance developer in Geelong, wrote a booking module for Moolap Reach Sailing School. Her contract assigned the copyright in the module's code to the sailing school. A year later, a kayak hire business asks Ines for a booking module with similar features. The sailing school hasn't given permission for its code to be reused. Which statement is most accurate?
options: She can copy the module's code, because she wrote every line of it
She can copy the module's code if she renames its variables and functions
She can copy the module's code, since the two businesses don't compete
She can write new code for similar features but not copy the old code
explanation: Assigning the copyright transferred ownership of the code to the sailing school, so Ines no longer has the right to copy it, even though she wrote it. Copyright protects the code, not the ideas behind it, so she can still write new code that provides similar features for the kayak hire business.
whyWrong: Writing the code made Ines its first owner, but her contract assigned the copyright to the sailing school.
Renamed code is still a copy of the sailing school's code, so she would still need its permission.
Copyright doesn't depend on whether the businesses compete; copying the code needs the owner's permission.

stem: Ironwood Driver Training, a driving school business covered by the Privacy Act 1988 (Cwlth), is having a booking program built. The developer plans to make each learner's learner permit number their learner ID: the key that identifies their record and is printed on receipts and lesson reminders. Which design best follows APP 9 (Adoption, use or disclosure of government related identifiers)?
options: Keep the permit number as each learner's ID, but encrypt it wherever it is stored
Keep the permit number as each learner's ID, but show only its last four digits
Give each learner a program-generated ID, using the permit number only to verify identity
Use each learner's Medicare number as their ID instead of their learner permit number
explanation: A learner permit number is a government related identifier: a number a government body has given the person. APP 9 stops an organisation adopting one as its own identifier for that person, so the program should create its own learner IDs. The school may still use the permit number where that is reasonably necessary to verify a learner's identity. A Victorian public sector body faces a similar limit under IPP 7 (Unique identifiers).
whyWrong: Encryption protects the stored number, which is APP 11's concern, but the school would still be adopting a government related identifier as its own ID.
Masking the number on screen still leaves it as the school's ID for each learner, which is what APP 9 restricts.
A Medicare number is also a government related identifier, so adopting it as the ID breaks the same principle.

stem: Yarrabee Shire Council in Victoria is designing an online application form for its youth leadership camp. Which proposed field would collect sensitive information under IPP 10 (Sensitive information)?
options: The applicant's religious beliefs, to plan activities around religious holidays
The applicant's date of birth, to check that they are aged 15 to 18
The applicant's school and year level, to place them in a camp group
The applicant's mobile number, to send reminders before the camp starts
explanation: Sensitive information is a narrower set of personal information: a person's racial or ethnic origin, political opinions or membership of a political association, religious or philosophical beliefs, membership of a professional or trade association or a union, sexual preferences or practices, or criminal record. IPP 10 lets the council collect it only in limited cases, such as with the applicant's consent or where a law requires it. The form should leave the field out unless it is really needed; if it is needed, the field should be optional and say why it is asked.
whyWrong: A date of birth is personal information, but not one of the sensitive categories; IPP 1 (Collection) still limits it to what the camp needs.
School and year level are personal information, but neither is in a sensitive category.
A mobile number is personal contact information, not sensitive information.

stem: A developer is naming the documents for a sports club's booking app. Which file name best follows a good file naming convention?
options: booking app SRS FINAL (2).docx
2026-03-14_bookingapp_srs_v1.2.docx
14-3-26_bookingapp_srs_latest.docx
srs_new_version_March_14th.docx
explanation: It names the project and the document, uses a sortable YYYY-MM-DD date and a version number, and avoids spaces and special characters.
whyWrong: 'FINAL (2)' isn't a real version, and the spaces and brackets can cause problems in some systems.
A day-first date doesn't sort in date order, and 'latest' stops being true once a newer file exists.
'new_version' isn't a version number, the project isn't named, and a written-out date doesn't sort.

stem: Spoonbill Plumbing in Sale keeps the project files for its job-scheduling program on an office computer. Every night the files are backed up to an external drive kept in the same office. A flood destroys both the computer and the drive. Which practice would have prevented the loss of the files?
options: Archiving completed job files to the external drive each month
Adding version numbers to the file names of every project document
Keeping a copy of the backup at a separate, off-site location
Switching from full backups to incremental backups each night
explanation: The backup was lost because it was kept in the same place as the originals. A copy held off-site would have survived the flood.
whyWrong: An archive on the same drive would have been destroyed with it.
Version numbers help identify files, but they don't create a copy that survives the flood.
Changing the type of backup doesn't change where it is kept, so it would still have been lost.

stem: Quokka Code, a software studio in Horsham, is replacing laptops that held copies of client databases used for testing. Before the laptops are sold, which action securely disposes of the client data?
options: Overwrite each drive with data-wiping software, or destroy the drives
Delete the project folders from each laptop, then empty the recycle bin
Archive the client databases to an external drive, then delete the originals
Rename the database files so that they no longer identify the client
explanation: Secure disposal means the data can't be recovered. Overwriting all of the data on each drive, or physically destroying the drive, achieves that; deleting files may leave the data recoverable.
whyWrong: Deleted files can often be recovered with free tools, because the data may remain on the drive.
Archiving keeps the data, and the deleted originals may still be recoverable from the laptops.
Renaming changes only the file names; the client data inside the files is untouched.

stem: Echidna Lane Software in Mildura makes a full backup of its code every Sunday night and an incremental backup on each of the other nights. The main drive fails on Friday morning. Which backups are needed to restore the files as they were on Thursday night?
options: Thursday night's incremental backup and nothing else
Sunday night's full backup, without any incrementals
Sunday's full backup and Thursday's incremental backup
Sunday's full backup and the four incrementals after it
explanation: Each incremental backup holds only the files changed since the previous backup. Restoring needs the full backup as the base, then the Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday incrementals applied in order.
whyWrong: Thursday's incremental holds only Thursday's changes; the unchanged files and earlier changes are missing.
The full backup alone loses every change made from Monday to Thursday.

Changes made on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday are held only in those nights' incrementals, so they would be lost. The full backup and the latest one alone would be enough only if the nightly backups were differential.

stem: Tyers Lane Software in Traralgon has finished a project for a client. The contract requires every copy of the client's customer data to be destroyed when the project ends. The studio has run data-wiping software over the development server that held the data. The server was backed up every night during the project, and the backups are stored on a separate drive. What else must the studio do to meet the contract?
options: Securely dispose of the customer data in the server's backups
Run one more full backup of the server so the deletion is recorded
Archive the backups to long-term storage in case the client asks
Rename the backup files so that they no longer name the client
explanation: Every nightly backup made during the project holds a copy of the customer data. Wiping the server leaves those copies untouched, so the studio must also securely dispose of the data in the backups, for example by wiping or destroying the backup drive once anything else on it that must be kept has been copied elsewhere.
whyWrong: A new backup doesn't remove the older backups, which still hold the customer data.
Archiving the backups keeps the customer data, which the contract says must be destroyed.
Renaming changes only the file names; the customer data inside the files is untouched.

stem: Elliminyt Web Studio in Colac finished a website for a football club three years ago. Nobody works on the project's files any more, but the studio's contract says they must be kept for seven years. The files take up space on the shared drive and clutter searches for current work. Which practice best suits these files?
options: Securely dispose of them so that they can't be recovered by anyone
Move them to an archive in long-term storage, off the shared drive
Back them up each night with an incremental backup on the shared drive
Rename them with version numbers so they sort after current projects
explanation: Archiving moves files that are no longer in active use to long-term storage. The files are kept for the seven years the contract requires, and the shared drive holds only current work. The archive may be the only copy, so it should itself be backed up.
whyWrong: The contract says the files must be kept for seven years, so destroying them now would breach it.
Backing the files up leaves them on the shared drive, so the clutter remains; files that no longer change need no nightly backup.
Renaming leaves the files on the shared drive, still taking up space.

stem: A two-person app studio in Kyabram backs up its project files to an external drive: a full backup every Saturday night and a differential backup on Monday to Friday nights. On Thursday morning, the main drive of the studio's computer fails. What is the smallest set of backups that will restore the files as they were on Wednesday night?
options: Wednesday night's differential backup on its own
Saturday night's full backup on its own
Saturday's full backup, then Wednesday's differential
Saturday's full backup, then all three differentials in order
explanation: A differential backup holds every file changed since the last full backup, so Wednesday's differential already contains Monday's and Tuesday's changes as well as Wednesday's. Restoring Saturday's full backup and then Wednesday's differential returns every file to its state on Wednesday night.
whyWrong: The differential holds only the files changed since Saturday; files that haven't changed since then exist only in the full backup.
The full backup alone loses every change made on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday.
This restores the files, but it isn't the smallest set: Wednesday's differential already includes Monday's and Tuesday's changes. Restoring a whole chain in order is what incremental backups need.

stem: Talia is designing a booking app for Tussock Point Cruises, a tour operator in Lakes Entrance. The owner wants the app to feel 'calm and coastal'. Talia gathers photographs of the lakes, sand and sea colour swatches, and samples of rounded fonts, and arranges them on one page so she and the owner can agree on a visual style. Which ideation tool has Talia created?
options: A mind map
A mock-up
A mood board
A brainstorm
explanation: A mood board collects images, colours, fonts and textures to capture the intended look and feel. It sets the visual style before any screen layout is designed.
whyWrong: A mind map branches out from a central topic to show how ideas relate; it isn't a collection of images and colours.
A mock-up shows the layout of a particular screen, not a collection of images, colours and fonts that sets a style.
A brainstorm is a session for generating many ideas; it doesn't arrange visual samples to set a style.

stem: At the first design meeting for a volunteer rostering program at Wirra Lane Community Kitchen in Bacchus Marsh, the project lead writes each suggestion on the whiteboard but stops to explain why most of them won't work. The meeting ends with only four ideas. Which change would best improve this brainstorm?
options: Record every suggestion and leave judging them until afterwards
Accept only suggestions that already meet the evaluation criteria
Replace the session with a detailed mock-up of the roster screen
Have the project lead choose the best idea as each one is suggested
explanation: Brainstorming depends on generating many ideas without judgement. Criticising ideas as they are made discourages people from suggesting more; evaluation belongs after the session.
whyWrong: Filtering ideas against criteria during the session is judging them early, which cuts the number of ideas.
A detailed mock-up specifies one screen after an idea has been chosen; it doesn't generate a range of ideas.
Choosing as ideas arrive is still judging during the session, which is the problem the meeting already has.

stem: Dev is planning a members' app for Quartzhill Rowing Club in Ballarat. He has a long list of possible features and wants to group them under headings such as training, racing and social events, showing how each feature connects to the others. Which ideation tool best suits this purpose?
options: A mood board
A sketch
A brainstorm
A mind map
explanation: A mind map is a structured diagram: the central topic sits in the middle, branches carry the groups of ideas, and further branches carry the individual ideas, so it shows how the features group and connect.
whyWrong: A mood board captures visual style, not how features group together.
A sketch explores a screen layout, not the relationships between features.
A brainstorm is an unstructured collection of ideas; Dev already has his list and needs to give it structure by grouping it.

stem: Kasey has sketched three alternative home screens for a click-and-collect app for Ridgeline Hardware in Wodonga. Before she produces a detailed design, what should she do next?
options: Write pseudocode for all three sketches so their logic can be compared
Evaluate each design idea against criteria to select a preferred design
Beta test each of the three sketches with a group of real customers
Draw a context diagram for each sketch to show the data it exchanges
explanation: Design ideas are compared against evaluation criteria so that the idea that best meets the requirements is chosen. Only the preferred design is then developed into a detailed design.
whyWrong: Pseudocode is a detailed design tool; writing it for every alternative wastes effort before one idea is chosen.
Beta testing is carried out on a developed solution, not on sketches of design ideas.
A context diagram is an analysis tool showing data flows with external entities; it doesn't compare screen designs.

stem: Hamid is generating design ideas for the home screen of a booking app for Wyuna Bend Houseboats in Echuca. He spends three days on a single sketch, drawing every icon precisely and matching each colour exactly, and plans to show only this sketch to the owners. What is the main problem with Hamid's approach?
options: Sketches should be drawn only after the detailed design is approved
A sketch of a screen should also give the pseudocode for each button
He polished one idea instead of quickly sketching several to compare
He should use a brainstorm, which records each idea in precise detail
explanation: Sketches are quick, rough drawings that let a designer explore several alternatives cheaply and compare them before committing to one. Three days spent perfecting one sketch leaves the owners nothing to compare it with. Exact icons and colours can be settled once a preferred design has been chosen and is being detailed.
whyWrong: Sketches are used while design ideas are generated, before a preferred design is chosen and detailed.
Pseudocode is a detailed design tool for processing; it isn't part of a sketch of a screen idea.
A brainstorm records many ideas quickly without judging them; it doesn't set out any idea in precise detail.

stem: Rafael has created a mood board for a members' app for Snowbrush Alpine Club in Mansfield. It holds photos of snow gums and alpine huts, a palette of deep green and white, and samples of a bold, rounded font. The club president asks Rafael to use the mood board to decide where the Book and Cancel buttons should go on each screen. What is the best response?
options: Use it, because a mood board shows where every control is placed
Brainstorm the positions, because a brainstorm settles the final layout
Add the buttons to the mood board so the president can approve them
Sketch the layouts; a mood board sets style, not control positions
explanation: A mood board captures the intended look and feel. It doesn't arrange anything on a screen, so it can't settle where buttons go. Sketches of alternative screen layouts are the tool for exploring placement, and the mood board's colours and fonts can then be applied to the chosen layout.
whyWrong: A mood board is a collection of images, colours and fonts; it doesn't lay out controls on a screen.
A brainstorm produces many ideas without judging them; it doesn't settle a final layout.
Adding buttons to a collage of images doesn't show where they sit on each screen; that needs a layout drawing.

stem: Mei has sketched two possible home screens for an app that lets members of a Warragul community garden book plots and tools. Before showing them to the garden's committee, she wants to write beside parts of each sketch why she made each choice, such as putting the plot map at the top of Sketch 1 because members check it most often, and to suggest that Sketch 2's tool-booking button could be added to Sketch 1. Which ideation technique or tool should Mei use?
options: A mind map linking the two sketches' ideas
Annotations added to each sketch
A mood board of garden photos and colours
A brainstorm with the garden's committee
explanation: Annotations are notes written on design ideas. Mei's notes would give the reason for a design choice, such as why the plot map sits at the top, and suggest a link between her two design ideas, such as moving a button from one sketch to the other.
whyWrong: A mind map shows how a set of ideas relate, branching out from a central theme; it doesn't put Mei's reasons on the sketches she has already drawn.
A mood board collects images, colours and fonts to set the design's direction; it doesn't explain the choices in a sketch.
A brainstorm gathers many new ideas without judging them; Mei is explaining and linking ideas she already has.

stem: Which of the following is a measure of the efficiency of a solution?
options: The accuracy of the totals shown on each invoice
The time taken to produce a month of invoices
Whether each invoice includes every required item
How readable the invoice layout is for customers
explanation: Efficiency concerns the resources used, such as time, cost and effort. The time taken to produce the invoices measures speed, so it is an efficiency measure.
whyWrong: Accuracy measures effectiveness: whether the output is correct.
Completeness measures effectiveness: whether the output contains everything required.
Readability measures effectiveness: how clearly the output communicates.

stem: Yabby Creek Pool Care in Shepparton replaced its paper service log with a tablet app. Before the change, about one service record in twenty had a wrong address or time. Since the change, staff take the same time as before to log a pool service, but the records have been error-free for three months. Which statement best describes the change?
options: The solution is more efficient because records are logged faster
The solution is less efficient because staff now use a tablet
The solution is more efficient because errors are now avoided
The solution is more effective because records are more accurate
explanation: Logging takes the same time, so efficiency hasn't changed. The records are now accurate, so the solution better achieves its purpose: an improvement in effectiveness.
whyWrong: The scenario says logging takes the same time as before, so speed hasn't improved.
Using a tablet doesn't by itself change the time, cost or effort, and nothing suggests efficiency fell.
Fewer errors means more accurate output, which is a gain in effectiveness, not efficiency.

stem: Mia is writing evaluation criteria for a stock-control program for Fernglade Nursery in Healesville. Which criterion is the most useful?
options: Staff can find any plant's stock level in under ten seconds
The program is easy for all nursery staff to use at work
The program is written in an object-oriented language
The program has an attractive and modern appearance
explanation: A useful criterion is specific and measurable, so it can be checked objectively. Finding a stock level in under ten seconds can be timed.
whyWrong: 'Easy to use' is vague: without a measure, different people will judge it differently.
This describes how the program is built, not how well it performs, so it can't judge efficiency or effectiveness.
'Attractive and modern' is a matter of opinion and can't be measured as written.

stem: Wattlebird Health Services in Bendigo replaced its payroll spreadsheet with a new program. Payroll now takes one hour each fortnight instead of five. However, the new program calculates some staff members' overtime incorrectly, which never happened with the spreadsheet. Compared with the spreadsheet, the new program is
options: more efficient and more effective.
less efficient and more effective.
more efficient and less effective.
less efficient and less effective.
explanation: Cutting payroll from five hours to one reduces time and effort, so the program is more efficient. Incorrect overtime means it achieves its purpose less well than the spreadsheet did, so it is less effective.
whyWrong: Wrong overtime calculations reduce accuracy, so the program is less effective, not more.
Payroll takes one hour instead of five, so the program is more efficient, not less.
The time saving makes the program more efficient; only its effectiveness has fallen.

stem:
One functional requirement for a fees program at Huon Creek Junior Soccer Club in Wodonga reads:

*The program calculates each player's season fee, taking $30 off when a brother or sister also plays at the club.*

Which evaluation criterion best judges how well the solution meets this requirement?
options: The fee screen shows each player's fee within two seconds of a search
Committee members agree that the fee screen looks clear and attractive
Every fee in a sample that includes siblings matches a hand calculation
The fee calculation is written as a function that can be reused next year
explanation: The requirement is about calculating fees correctly, including the sibling discount. Checking every fee in a sample that includes siblings against a hand calculation is specific and measurable, and it checks exactly what the requirement asks for.
whyWrong: Speed is worth measuring, but it doesn't show whether the fees, including the sibling discount, are correct.
Clarity and attractiveness are effectiveness measures, but this criterion says nothing about whether the fees, including the sibling discount, are calculated correctly.
This describes how the program is built, not how well it meets the requirement.

stem: Campaspe Crust Bakery in Kyneton trades seven days a week. Its new program produces a weekly report listing each day's sales, and the office manager produces it in about 20 seconds without help. When the owner checks the first report against the till receipts, every figure in it is correct, but Saturday and Sunday are missing. Which evaluation criterion does the report fail?
options: The report includes sales for every day on which the bakery trades
Every sales figure shown in the report matches the bakery's till receipts
The weekly report can be produced in less than one minute
The office manager can produce the report without any help
explanation: Every figure the report shows is accurate, but two trading days are missing, so the report is incomplete. Completeness is a measure of effectiveness: the output must include everything that is required.
whyWrong: The owner found that every figure shown was correct, so the report meets this accuracy criterion.
The report takes about 20 seconds, well under a minute, so it meets this criterion.
The office manager produces the report without help, so it meets this criterion.

stem: Saltpan Freight in Laverton has a new program that produces a weekly report of late deliveries. The depot managers discuss the report at a meeting at 9 am every Monday. Which evaluation criterion measures the report's effectiveness rather than its efficiency?
options: The report is generated in 3 seconds, down from 40 seconds
The office manager spends 2 minutes a week on it, down from 20
Running the report costs under $2 a week in server charges
Every depot manager has the report before the Monday meeting
explanation: Timeliness is one of the study design's measures of effectiveness: the report is timely when it is available by the time it is needed, here the Monday meeting. How fast it is generated, how much staff time it takes and what it costs to run are the time, effort and cost used to produce it, which are measures of efficiency.
whyWrong: Speed of processing is a measure of efficiency. A report generated in 3 seconds on Monday afternoon would be fast but still too late for the meeting.
Less of the office manager's time spent on the report is a saving in time and effort, which makes it more efficient, not more effective.
The cost of running the report is a measure of efficiency, not of how well the report serves the managers.

stem: Oren is building a lesson booking program for Sandspit Surf School in Inverloch. In the design stage, he wrote evaluation criteria based on the requirements and used them to choose his preferred design idea. While coding, he reworded one criterion so that it could be measured more precisely. The program has now been in use for two months. How should Oren evaluate it, following the problem-solving methodology?
options: Write new criteria that match the features the finished program turned out to have
Apply the criteria from design, including the reworded one, to judge efficiency and effectiveness
Apply the criteria exactly as first written in design, undoing the change made while coding
Re-run the testing table from development, since passing every test shows the requirements are met
explanation: The problem-solving methodology uses one set of criteria throughout. They are developed in the design stage from the requirements and used to choose the preferred design, they can be adjusted while the program is being built, and the same criteria are then applied in the evaluation stage to judge how efficient and effective the finished program is.
whyWrong: Criteria written to fit the finished program would only confirm what it already does. The program is judged against the criteria based on its requirements.
Criteria may be sharpened during development, so the more measurable wording should be kept, not undone.
Testing checks during development that the program works as expected. Evaluation applies the criteria to data from the program in use to judge its efficiency and effectiveness.

stem: Jarrah is preparing the data dictionary below for a registration program for Kulkyne Netball Club in Mildura. Which entry has the least suitable data type?
options: playerName, because a name should be stored as a Character
teamGrade, because a grade should be stored as an Integer
hasPaid, because a payment status should be stored as a String
gamesPlayed, because a count of games should be stored as an Integer
explanation: A count of games is always a whole number, so Integer suits it. Floating point is for values that can have a fractional part, such as a fee in dollars and cents.
whyWrong: A Character holds a single character; a full name needs a String, which is what the entry uses.
A grade from A to D is a single letter that isn't used in arithmetic, so Character suits it.
Paid or not paid has exactly two states, so Boolean suits it better than a String.

figures.title: Data dictionary: player registration
rows: Grade of the player's team, A to D
Whether the season fee has been paid
Number of games played this season

stem: The mock-up below is part of the detailed design for a class booking program at Stonebridge Fitness in Bendigo. The developer is writing the object description for a Booking object. Which property would best store the data captured by the "Hire a towel" control?
options: towelHire, with the data type String
towelHire, with the data type Boolean
towelHire(), listed as a method
towelHire, with the data type Floating point
explanation: A check box is either ticked or not, so the data it captures has exactly two states. Boolean is the most suitable data type for a property that stores it.
whyWrong: A String could hold "yes" or "no" but allows other values too; Boolean matches the two states of a check box.
The check box captures data to be stored, so it belongs in a property, not a method.
The check box records whether a towel is hired, not an amount; the $3 fee is fixed and needn't be captured.

stem: The pseudocode below is part of the detailed design for Blowhole Bay Tours in Warrnambool. It calculates the total fare for a booking group. Arrays are indexed from 0. What value is displayed?
explanation: The loop adds 40 (age 34), 25 (age 12), 30 (age 67), 25 (age 8) and 40 (age 41), giving 160. Because 160 > 150, line 14 subtracts 10, so 150 is displayed.
whyWrong: This total leaves out one passenger; the loop runs from 0 to LENGTH(ages) - 1, which covers all five.
This is the total before the discount; 160 is greater than 150, so 10 is subtracted.
This charges the 67-year-old the adult fare and skips the discount; 67 >= 65, so the fare is 30.

figures.code:
BEGIN
    ages ← [34, 12, 67, 8, 41]
    total ← 0
    FOR i ← 0 TO LENGTH(ages) - 1
        IF ages[i] < 16 THEN
            total ← total + 25
        ELSEIF ages[i] >= 65 THEN
            total ← total + 30
        ELSE
            total ← total + 40
        ENDIF
    ENDFOR
    IF total > 150 THEN
        total ← total - 10
    ENDIF
    DISPLAY total
END

stem: Hamish drew the IPO chart below for a module that calculates a casual worker's pay for one shift at Quillmoor Café in Ballarat. The chart is missing an input. Which input should be added?
options: The day of the week on which the shift was worked
The shift pay calculated for the worker's shift
A step that calculates the Sunday loading
The worker's total pay for the whole week
explanation: The processing decides whether to add a Sunday loading, so the module needs to know which day the shift was worked. Without that input, the decision can't be made.
whyWrong: Shift pay is the result the module produces, so it belongs in the Output column.
Calculating the loading is an action, so it belongs in the Process column, not the Input column.
Weekly pay isn't used to calculate one shift's pay, so it isn't an input to this module.

figures.title: IPO chart: shift pay
rows: Multiply hoursWorked by hourlyRate to get shiftPay
If the shift was on a Sunday, add a 25% loading to shiftPay

stem: The pseudocode below is part of the detailed design for Yapeen Ridge Firewood in Castlemaine. It works out how many truck trips are needed to deliver a day's orders, in the order they were placed. Each order is measured in cubic metres, and the truck carries at most 10 cubic metres. Arrays are indexed from 0. What value is displayed?
explanation: The first load is 6 + 3 = 9. Adding 5 would make 14, which is over 10, so a trip is counted and the next load starts with 5. Adding 8 would make 13, so a second trip is counted and the next load starts with 8. Adding 2 makes exactly 10, which isn't over 10, so it fits. After the loop, lines 14 to 16 count the last load as the third trip, so 3 is displayed.
whyWrong: This leaves out lines 14 to 16: the last load of 10 cubic metres still needs a trip after the loop ends.
This treats 8 + 2 = 10 as too much; line 7 tests for more than 10, so a load of exactly 10 fits.
This gives every order its own trip; line 11 adds each order to the current load while the total stays within 10.

figures.code:
BEGIN
    orders ← [6, 3, 5, 8, 2]
    load ← 0
    trips ← 0
    i ← 0
    WHILE i < LENGTH(orders) DO
        IF load + orders[i] > 10 THEN
            trips ← trips + 1
            load ← 0
        ENDIF
        load ← load + orders[i]
        i ← i + 1
    ENDWHILE
    IF load > 0 THEN
        trips ← trips + 1
    ENDIF
    DISPLAY trips
END

stem: The IPO chart and data dictionary below are part of the detailed design for a module at Dollarbird Flat Caravan Park in Robinvale. The module calculates the cost of a stay. Which change should be made to the data dictionary?

Add calculateCost, with the data type Floating point
Add isMember, with the data type Boolean
Change the data type of totalCost to Integer
explanation: isMember is an input in the IPO chart but has no entry in the data dictionary, and every data item a module uses should appear there. A guest either is or isn't a member, and the process tests whether isMember is true, so Boolean suits it.
whyWrong: isMember is needed, but it has exactly two states and the process tests whether it is true, so Boolean suits it better than String.
Calculating the cost is processing, not a data item, so it doesn't belong in the data dictionary.
Costs can include cents: 3 nights for a member is $121.50, so totalCost must stay Floating point.

stem: Myrtlebank Vets in Ballarat is adding a feature to its appointment app. After booking, clients can add the appointment to the calendar app on their phone with one tap, using a standard calendar file format. Which user experience characteristic does this feature most directly improve?
options: Interoperability
Affordance
Security
Portability
explanation: The app exchanges data with a different program, the phone's calendar, in a format both can use. Working with other systems in this way is interoperability.
whyWrong: Affordance is about an element's appearance suggesting how to use it, not about exchanging data with other programs.
Security protects data and accounts; sharing an appointment with the calendar doesn't make anything more secure.
Portability means running on different platforms and isn't one of the four UX characteristics; this feature exchanges data with another program.

stem: During testing of a food-ordering app for Quandong Lane Bakehouse in Echuca, several users didn't realise they could tap a product photo to see its ingredients. The photos have no border, icon or other cue. Which change best addresses this problem?
options: Encrypt the ingredient data so that it is transmitted securely
Export the ingredient list in a format other apps can read
Add a visible cue, such as an "Ingredients" button, to each photo
Make sure the app runs on both Android and iOS phones
explanation: The photos have poor affordance: nothing in their appearance suggests they can be tapped. A visible cue such as a labelled button tells users the element is interactive.
whyWrong: Encryption improves security, but the users' problem is not knowing the photo can be tapped.
Exporting data improves interoperability, which doesn't help users discover the tap action.
Running on more platforms improves portability; users on every platform would still miss the tap action.

stem: Coolabah Credit Co-operative in Shepparton has a members' app that currently needs only a password. The co-operative plans to add a one-time code, sent to each member's phone, at every sign-in. Which statement best describes the likely effect on the user experience?
options: Usability improves, because members have another way to prove who they are
Security improves, but the extra step at each sign-in may reduce usability
Interoperability improves, because the app now works with members' phones
Affordance improves, because the sign-in screen now shows more controls
explanation: A one-time code makes it much harder for someone with a stolen password to sign in, so security improves. It also adds a step every time, which can frustrate members, so the design should keep that effort low.
whyWrong: An extra sign-in step adds effort for members, so it tends to reduce usability, not improve it.
The code is a security measure; interoperability is about exchanging data with other systems, which this change doesn't add.
Affordance concerns whether controls look usable; adding a control doesn't improve that.

stem: Passengers aged over 70 who use a booking app for Tarwin Community Transport in Leongatha report that the text is too small to read and that booking a seat takes seven screens. Which change most directly addresses these reports?
options: Store every booking in an encrypted database
Let bookings be exported to other transport apps
Give each button a shadow so it looks raised
Enlarge the text and cut the number of screens
explanation: Both reports concern how easily users can use the app. Larger text and fewer screens make booking easier to read and simpler to follow, which improves usability.
whyWrong: Encryption improves security but doesn't make the text larger or the booking shorter.
Exporting bookings improves interoperability, which doesn't address small text or too many screens.
Shading buttons improves affordance, but the users' problems are small text and too many steps.

stem: Tuckers Bend Library in Kerang has a kiosk where borrowers sign in to renew loans and see their borrowing history, address and phone number. Borrowers know how to sign out, but staff often find that a borrower has walked away still signed in. Which change best improves the kiosk's security for borrowers?
options: Make the Sign out button larger and shade it so that it looks pressable
Enlarge the text on every screen and cut the steps needed to renew a loan
Sign the borrower out automatically after a minute without activity
Let borrowers export their loan history to a calendar or spreadsheet
explanation: While a borrower stays signed in, the next person at the kiosk could see their address and phone number or change their loans. Signing out automatically after a short idle time protects each borrower even when they forget, and adds no steps for those who remember.
whyWrong: Borrowers already know how to sign out; a more visible button doesn't help when they forget to use it.
This improves usability, but the next person could still see a signed-in borrower's details.
Exporting data improves interoperability and does nothing about accounts left signed in.

stem: Volunteers at Toolleen Wildlife Rescue near Elmore log each animal rescue in a phone app. In testing, every volunteer could see at once which buttons and boxes to use on each screen. However, logging one rescue took most volunteers over four minutes, because several of the app's nine screens ask for the same details again, and some volunteers gave up before finishing. Which characteristic of the user experience most needs improving?
options: Affordance, because volunteers can't tell which controls they should use
Usability, because logging a rescue takes too long and too many steps
Interoperability, because the same details must be entered more than once
Security, because a rescue is lost if a volunteer gives up partway
explanation: Usability is how easily users can learn and operate a solution to complete their tasks. The volunteers could tell how to use every control, so affordance isn't the problem; the task itself is slow, repeats details and makes some volunteers give up. Asking for each detail once, on fewer screens, would improve usability.
whyWrong: Testers found that every volunteer could see at once which buttons and boxes to use, so the controls already show how they are used.
The details are asked for again within this one app. Interoperability is about exchanging data with other programs, and no other program is involved.
An unfinished record is lost because the task is too long, not because anyone gains access to data or accounts, which is what security protects against.

stem: The mock-up below shows the draft Hire a bike screen for a self-service kiosk at Spotted Gum Bike Hire in Bright. Customers have already signed in on the previous screen. When customers tried a prototype, many couldn't work out what to type in each box or what the button would do. Which characteristic of user experience most needs improving?
options: Affordance
Contrast
Security
Portability
explanation: Affordance is how clearly an element's appearance shows what it is for and how to use it. Boxes with no label or hint text, and a button showing only a symbol, give customers no cue about what to enter or what will happen. Labelling the boxes (for example "Bike number" and "Hours of hire") and naming the button "Hire this bike" would improve affordance.
whyWrong: Contrast is a design principle, not a characteristic of user experience. Making the boxes and button stand out more still wouldn't tell customers what they are for.
Customers have already signed in, and their problem is working out what each control is for, not protecting their account or data.
Portability is a non-functional requirement about running on different platforms, not one of the four characteristics of user experience.

elements.note: Neither box has a label or hint text
The button shows only the » symbol

stem: In a rostering app for Pelican Bay Surf Club in Anglesea, the button that confirms a shift is green and labelled "Confirm" on one screen, blue and labelled "OK" on another, and orange and labelled "Accept" on a third. Volunteers say they have to hunt for the button on each screen. Which design principle has been applied poorly?
options: Alignment
Contrast
Usability
Affordance
explanation: The same action has a different colour and label on each screen, so volunteers can't learn what to look for and must search every time, which makes the app harder to use. Usability (ease of use) is a design principle as well as a UX characteristic; here, applying it means giving the confirm button one colour and one label on every screen.
whyWrong: Alignment is about lining elements up; the problem is that the same button changes colour and wording.
Contrast makes important elements stand out; each button is a strong colour, and the problem is that one action looks different on each screen.
Affordance is a characteristic of user experience, not a design principle, and each version still looks like a button that can be pressed.

stem: Passengers using a timetable app for Ridgeway Coachlines in Horsham complain that the departure times, shown in pale yellow text on a white background, are hard to read outdoors. Which change best applies a design principle to fix this?
options: Align the departure times with the left edge of the screen
Show the departure times in the same font as the headings
Move the departure times onto a separate screen of their own
Show departure times in dark text on the white background
explanation: Pale yellow on white has very low contrast. Dark text on a light background increases contrast, so the times stay readable even in bright light.
whyWrong: Alignment changes where the times sit, not how readable pale text is against white.
Changing the font leaves the text pale yellow, so the times would still be hard to read against white.
Moving the times doesn't change their colour, so the low contrast remains.

stem: The mock-up below shows a membership form for Whipstick Chess Club in Bendigo. Which design principle is most clearly not applied?
options: Alignment
Text formatting
Interoperability
Contrast
explanation: The labels and text boxes start at a different horizontal position on each row, so there is no shared edge. Lining them up in two columns would make the form faster to scan and complete.
whyWrong: Nothing on the form points to a text formatting problem; the heading and labels are readable. The problem is where each row starts.
Interoperability is a characteristic of user experience about exchanging data with other systems, not a design principle, and a form's layout doesn't show it.
Contrast concerns making elements distinct; the problem is that the fields don't line up.

stem: Farida is designing a document editor for Lindqvist Legal in Mildura. To keep the toolbar looking uniform, she gives the "Delete document" button exactly the same colour, size and style as the "Save" button, and places the two side by side. Why is this a poor design decision?
options: Two buttons can't share a row without breaking alignment
Delete does another job, so it should contrast with Save
Text formatting needs each button label in its own font
Matching styles stops the buttons from looking pressable
explanation: Delete and Save do different things, and a deleted document may be hard to recover. Making Delete contrast with Save, for example with a different colour or an outlined style, lets users tell them apart at a glance, so Delete isn't pressed by mistake. Matching styles suit buttons that do the same job, not these two.
whyWrong: Buttons can share a row and still be aligned; alignment isn't the issue here.
Text formatting doesn't call for a different font on each label; one font for every button label is normal. The risk is that Delete can't be told apart from Save.
Both still look like buttons, so their affordance is unchanged; the issue is telling them apart.

stem: On the online enrolment form for Goulburn Bend Swim School in Seymour, required fields are marked only by showing their labels in red instead of black. Some parents with colour blindness say the red and black labels look the same to them. Which change best applies contrast to fix this?
options: Show the required labels in a brighter shade of red than before
Line up every label and text box along one shared left edge
Use the same red for required labels on every screen of the form
Also mark required labels with bold type and an asterisk
explanation: Contrast can come from weight, size and shape as well as colour. Bold type and an asterisk make required labels stand out for every user, including parents who can't tell the two colours apart.
whyWrong: A different red still relies on colour alone, which these parents can't distinguish.
Alignment makes the form easier to scan, but it doesn't show which fields are required.
Using red consistently still relies on colour alone, so these parents still can't see the difference.

stem: The price list screen of a stock program for Koorlong Irrigation Supplies in Mildura shows prices such as $8.50, $112.00 and $1,245.90 centred in their column. Staff say they often misjudge at a glance which prices are large. Which change best applies a design principle to fix this?
options: Show the prices in bold type so that they stand out from item names
Right-align the prices so that their decimal points line up
Use the same font and colour for prices on every screen
Centre the column heading as well, so the column is symmetrical
explanation: Every price has two decimal places, so right-aligning the column lines up digits of the same place value, and a larger price visibly extends further to the left. Staff can then compare prices at a glance. This applies alignment.
whyWrong: Bold type adds contrast with the item names, but centred prices still don't line up by place value.
Matching the font and colour across screens is a text formatting choice, but it doesn't change how the prices line up within this column.
Centring the heading leaves the prices centred, so their digits still don't line up.

stem: Guests book a powered site at Lowan Springs Caravan Park near Dimboola through a five-screen online form. In testing, guests couldn't tell how many screens were left. When one guest reached the third screen and wanted to change her dates, the form gave her no way back to the first screen, so she had to start again. Which design principle has been applied poorly?
options: Alignment
Balance
Navigation
Text formatting
explanation: Navigation is how users find their way around a solution and move between its screens. A step indicator such as "Step 3 of 5" would show guests where they are, and a Back button on every screen would let them return to an earlier step without losing what they have entered.
whyWrong: Alignment lines elements up along shared edges; the guests' problems are knowing where they are and getting back, not where elements sit.
Balance spreads visual weight evenly across a screen; an even layout wouldn't show guests how many screens are left or let them go back.
Text formatting makes text readable and shows what matters; the guests could read each screen but couldn't move between the screens.

stem: The study design relates each of its design principles to a solution's functionality, its usability or its appearance. Which of these is one of the principles it relates to appearance?
options: Balance
Navigation
Proximity
Affordance
explanation: The study design relates alignment, balance, contrast, image use, space, and text and table formatting to appearance. Balance is about spreading visual weight evenly across a screen.
whyWrong: Navigation is a design principle, but the study design relates it, with interactivity, to functionality rather than appearance.
Proximity isn't one of the study design's design principles; keeping related items together and separating groups is part of applying space.
Affordance is a characteristic of user experience, not a design principle.
